summary: Judas leads an armed crowd to Gethsemane and betrays Jesus with a kiss; Jesus gives Himself up, heals a wounded servant, and His disciples flee.
key_insight: When Jesus said, “I am He,” the armed men drew back and fell to the ground. They could not have taken Him unless He let them. Then He bargained, not for Himself, but for His disciples: “let these go their way.”
story: While Jesus was still speaking, Judas, one of the twelve, arrived. He knew the place, for Jesus often met there with His disciples. {Jn} With him came a great multitude with swords and clubs from the chief priests, the scribes and the elders, {Mk} a detachment of troops and officers with lanterns, torches, and weapons. {Jn}

Judas had given them a signal: “Whomever I kiss, He is the One; seize Him and lead Him away safely.” {Mk} He went straight up to Jesus, said, “Greetings, Rabbi!” and kissed Him. {Mt} Jesus said to him, “Friend, why have you come?” {Mt} and “Judas, are you betraying the Son of Man with a kiss?” {Lk}

Knowing all that would come upon Him, Jesus went forward and asked, “Whom are you seeking?” They answered, “Jesus of Nazareth.” He said, “I am He.” Judas was standing with them. At those words they drew back and fell to the ground. Again He asked, and again they said, “Jesus of Nazareth.” “I have told you that I am He,” He answered. “Therefore, if you seek Me, let these go their way.” {Jn}

As they laid hands on Him, the disciples asked, “Lord, shall we strike with the sword?” {Lk} Simon Peter drew his sword, struck the high priest’s servant, and cut off his right ear. The servant’s name was Malchus. {Jn} Jesus said, “Permit even this,” and He touched his ear and healed him. {Lk}

To Peter He said, “Put your sword into the sheath. Shall I not drink the cup which My Father has given Me?” {Jn} “All who take the sword will perish by the sword.” He could pray to His Father, and He would send more than twelve legions of angels. “How then could the Scriptures be fulfilled, that it must happen thus?” {Mt}

Then He turned to the chief priests, the captains of the temple and the elders. {Lk} “Have you come out, as against a robber, with swords and clubs to take Me? I sat daily with you, teaching in the temple, and you did not seize Me.” {Mt} “But this is your hour, and the power of darkness.” {Lk} The troops, their captain and the officers arrested Jesus and bound Him. {Jn}

Then all the disciples forsook Him and fled. A young man was following Him with only a linen cloth thrown around his body. When they seized him, he left the cloth behind and fled from them naked. {Mk}
differences: Only John records Jesus stepping forward, saying “I am He,” and the arresting party falling to the ground. John does not mention the kiss.
Jesus’ words to Judas differ: “Friend, why have you come?” (Matthew) and “Judas, are you betraying the Son of Man with a kiss?” (Luke). Mark records no words.
Only John names Peter as the swordsman and Malchus as the servant. Luke and John say it was the right ear; only Luke records the healing.
Jesus’ rebuke differs: the sword and the twelve legions (Matthew), “Permit even this” (Luke), and the cup (John).
Only Luke records “this is your hour, and the power of darkness.” Only Mark tells of the young man who fled naked.

fit.question: Why did Judas need to identify Jesus with a kiss if Jesus stepped forward and said, “I am He”? Which came first?

points.label: The kiss first
points.text: Mark says Judas went up to Jesus “as soon as he had come” (Mark 14:45). John says that when Jesus said “I am He,” Judas “also stood with them” (John 18:5), which fits Judas having given the sign and stepped back. Jesus then made plain that He would not hide.

points.label: Or “I am He” first
points.text: McGarvey placed John’s scene first: Jesus named Himself twice before Judas could act, and Judas went ahead with the kiss anyway. The prearranged signal was carried out as planned.

fit.note: John adds what the others leave out; he does not deny the kiss. The order is not stated, and either order fits all four accounts.
fit.short: No Gospel gives the order. Judas may have kissed Jesus on arrival before Jesus stepped forward, or the reverse. Either order fits.

scene.label: The arresting party
scene.text: John’s word for the “detachment of troops” is the term for a Roman cohort, nominally about six hundred men, and its “captain” is a commander of a thousand. Probably a body of Roman soldiers from the Antonia Fortress came with the temple police, though some think John means only the temple guard.

scene.label: Lanterns at full moon
scene.text: Passover fell at the full moon, yet the crowd brought lanterns and torches. The olive grove lay in the shadow of the Mount of Olives, and they may have expected to search for a man in hiding.

scene.label: The kiss
scene.text: A kiss was a common greeting, and a disciple might greet his teacher this way. Judas used the sign of honor and affection as the signal for arrest. Proverbs 27:6 says, “the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.”

scene.label: Twelve legions
scene.text: A Roman legion had about six thousand soldiers, so twelve legions would be more than seventy thousand angels. The Man facing a cohort had heaven’s armies at His call.

scene.label: The young man
scene.text: Only Mark tells this. Many have thought it was Mark himself, whose mother’s house in Jerusalem was a gathering place for the disciples (Acts 12:12). Mark does not say, and the man’s name stays hidden.

witnesses.matthew: Shows Jesus in command of the moment. He calls Judas “Friend,” forbids the sword, and says He could ask for twelve legions of angels. Twice He says this is happening so that the Scriptures would be fulfilled (26:54, 56).
witnesses.mark: Is brief and stark: a signal, a kiss, an arrest, and then “they all forsook Him and fled.” Only Mark adds the young man who ran away naked, a detail with no clear purpose except that someone remembered it, possibly Mark himself.
witnesses.luke: Records Jesus naming the betrayal for what it was, a kiss used to hand over the Son of Man. Luke alone tells of the healing of the servant’s ear, the last healing before the cross, done for a man who came to arrest Him.
witnesses.john: Shows the soldiers falling back at “I am He,” words Jesus had used of Himself before (John 8:24, 28). John names Peter and Malchus, records Jesus’ word about the cup, and shows Jesus shielding His disciples so that His word would be fulfilled: “Of those whom You gave Me I have lost none” (18:9).

seeing.reveals: Jesus is not captured; He gives Himself up. He steps forward, names Himself, shields His friends, heals His enemy’s ear, and lets Himself be bound.
seeing.living: Peter reached for a sword to defend a kingdom that would never come by swords. Jesus’ cause is served by His ways, by truth, mercy and trust in the Father, not by force. And when fear makes us run, as all the disciples did, He has already said, “let these go their way.”
seeing.ponder: Where are you reaching for a sword when Jesus is asking you to trust the cup the Father has given?

preaching.big_idea: Jesus was not taken by force; He stepped forward and gave Himself up to save His own.
outline: A betrayer who knew the place (2–3)
A Shepherd who shields His sheep (7–9)
A Son who drinks the cup (10–12)
preaching.watch_for: John 18:9 quotes Jesus’ prayer from earlier that night (17:12). Within the hour of asking the Father to keep His own, Jesus keeps them Himself by trading His freedom for theirs.

title: Betrayed and Arrested
